pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–8 years

- **Topic:** Friction & Surfaces

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, Year 3 Forces and Magnets):** Compare how things move on different surfaces.

- **Standards — US (NGSS — no discrete elementary PE; friction excluded from the K-PS2 boundary):** Friction is not assessed as a standalone elementary performance expectation — the K-PS2-2 assessment boundary explicitly excludes [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-PS2-2]; friction-as-a-force is treated qualitatively and connects to 3-PS2-1, then is formalised at MS-PS2.

- **Operational details:** Children compare how the SAME object moves across different surfaces (carpet, polished wood, sandpaper, ice) and discover that some surfaces produce more friction than others — rough surfaces slow things more than smooth. The key conceptual upgrade is to treat friction as a FORCE acting between two surfaces to oppose their motion, not merely as a property of 'rough things'. The Institute of Physics frames this for primary/lower-secondary as grip (friction that prevents sliding) and slip (friction that slows sliding, and warms the surfaces). Because friction can't be seen, it must be represented with force arrows ('forces spectacles'). The comparison is naturally a fair test: keep the object the same, change only the surface, measure how far it travels.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational).
bestPractices: Hands-on comparison: send the same object across at least three surfaces and measure distance travelled, keeping everything else the same (links to fair testing / pattern-seeking).
Name friction as a FORCE that opposes motion and represent it with an arrow pointing against the movement ('forces spectacles'), since friction is invisible (IOP).
Use the IOP grip/slip framing and a warming demonstration (rub hands together; feel a surface warm under sliding) to make the invisible force tangible — slip warms things, grip does not.
Foreground friction as the REASON things slow and stop, directly countering the 'force runs out' impetus idea.
Clean the variable: compare smoothness/roughness, and beware confounds — 'shiny' is not the same as 'low friction', and rolling must not be compared with sliding.
Discuss friction as both helpful (grip lets us walk, brakes work) and unhelpful (slows a sledge) so it isn't cast as simply 'bad'.
keyRepresentations: Multi-surface runway/ramp with one object and a distance scale
Force arrow opposing motion ('forces spectacles' — making the invisible friction visible)
Grip vs slip labelling of frictional forces (IOP)
Warming demonstration (rubbing hands / surfaces) to feel slip dissipating energy
commonMisconceptions: Friction is a phenomenon or a 'thing', not named/treated as a force (IOP).
Friction only acts when things move (slip) — or the mirror error, only when things are still (grip); both are partial views (IOP).
Friction is always bad/undesirable, ignoring that grip is what lets us walk and brake.
Things stop because the push/force 'runs out', rather than because friction pushes back (impetus link).
Confusing smoothness with shininess ('shiny = slippery'); and comparing rolling resistance with sliding as if they were the same.
Reasoning backwards from effect to cause — 'it took a long time to stop, so the friction must have been small' (IOP tripwire).

learn.summary: For 7–8 year olds, teach friction as a FORCE between two surfaces that opposes sliding motion, not merely a property of 'rough things'. Central activity: send the SAME object across several surfaces (ice, polished wood, carpet, sandpaper) as a fair test, measure distance travelled, and represent the invisible friction with a force arrow pointing against the motion. Use the Institute of Physics grip/slip framing, connect slip to warming, and confront the 'push runs out' impetus idea plus the 'shiny = slippery' confusion. For grip (static friction), be clear it balances an applied push or a slope's pull — a still object with nothing pushing it has no horizontal friction. Includes consolidation sorting/ordering, an annotated real-world reference, and a two-tier diagnostic.

activities.title: Same object, different surfaces: a fair-test friction runway
feedback: If the object stops sooner on carpet than on polished wood, ask: what was the only thing you changed? The surface. So the surface is what made the difference.
If a learner changed the object or the push between runs, point out the test is no longer fair — reset and vary only the surface.
Praise predicting first: comparing your prediction to the measured distance is how a pattern ('rougher = stops sooner') emerges from your own trials rather than being told.
activities.rationale: Comparing one object across multiple surfaces with distance measured supports pattern-seeking and fair testing, and gives direct evidence that the surface is the causal variable. Representing the comparison with accumulated data makes the trend visible.
sourceClaims: Rough surfaces have more friction than smooth surfaces; lubricants reduce friction; sliding rough surfaces past each other has a warming effect (slip is dissipative, grip is not).
learnerActions: Set up a flat runway (physical track, or a screen simulation of one) and choose one object (e.g. a puck or wooden block) that you will NOT change between runs.
Before each run, predict how far the object will travel and mark your predicted stopping point.

Give the object the same push each time (e.g. release it from the same point on a small launch ramp or pull back a rubber band by the same amount, since hand flicks vary), send it across at least three different surfaces in turn (e.g. ice/very smooth, polished wood, carpet, sandpaper), repeat each run a few times, and keep everything else the same so only the surface changes.
Measure and record how far it travelled on each surface in a data table (surface ↔ distance), and build up a simple bar chart so the pattern becomes visible.
Order the surfaces from 'object travels furthest' to 'stops soonest' and describe the pattern in your own words.
activities.intendedInsight: Changing only the surface changes how far the same pushed object travels before it slows to a stop: rougher surfaces produce more friction and stop the object sooner. This is a fair test — keep the object and the push the same, change only the surface.

activities.title: Forces spectacles: drawing the invisible friction arrow
feedback: If a learner points the arrow the way the object is moving, ask which way the push that SLOWS it must point — against the motion.
If a learner calls friction 'the rough bits' or 'stickiness', re-voice it as a force: the surfaces rubbing push back on the object.
Linking arrow length to the measured stopping distance helps: the surface where it stopped soonest gets the longest backward arrow.
activities.rationale: Friction cannot be seen, so a force-arrow representation ('forces spectacles') makes it tangible and names it explicitly as a force opposing motion, addressing the phenomenon-not-force misconception.
sourceClaims: Many students see friction as a phenomenon rather than as a force; when two surfaces are in contact there is a force on each surface acting to stop them moving past one another.

The friction misconception has two mirror forms (friction only when moving / only when still); IOP teaches grip (prevents sliding, e.g. lets us walk) and slip (slows sliding and warms surfaces); friction can't be shown as a concrete entity so use force arrows; avoid reasoning backwards from effect to cause.
learnerActions: After a run, draw a force arrow on the moving object pointing BACKWARDS, against the direction it is sliding — this represents the friction slowing it.
Compare runs: draw a short arrow for a smooth surface and a longer arrow for a rough surface, matching 'more friction = longer arrow'.
Say out loud which way friction pushes and why the object slows: friction is a force from the surfaces acting against the sliding motion.
Optionally, in a screen simulation, toggle a 'forces spectacles' overlay that shows the opposing arrow growing longer on rougher surfaces, and watch a warming meter glow on the rough, sliding runs.
activities.intendedInsight: Friction is a force acting between two surfaces in contact, opposing their sliding. Though invisible, it can be represented by an arrow pointing against the motion; it is larger on rougher surfaces, which is why the object slows and stops sooner.

activities.title: Grip and slip, and the warming you can feel
feedback: If a learner says a still object never has friction: a block with nothing pushing it has no horizontal friction, but push it (or place it on a slope) and it still does not slide — static (grip) friction is balancing that push before any motion.
If a learner says friction is 'bad', ask how we would walk or stop a bike without it.
Feeling hands warm gives a direct sensation of slip dissipating energy — the screen can show a warming meter but cannot let you feel it.
activities.rationale: The grip/slip framing counters both mirror forms of the misconception (friction only when moving / only when still) and the 'friction is always bad' view; the warming experience grounds the energy aspect of slip. Scoping grip to an applied push or slope keeps the static-friction physics correct.
sourceClaims: The friction misconception has two mirror forms (friction only when moving / only when still); IOP teaches grip (prevents sliding, e.g. lets us walk) and slip (slows sliding and warms surfaces); friction can't be shown as a concrete entity so use force arrows; avoid reasoning backwards from effect to cause.
Rough surfaces have more friction than smooth surfaces; lubricants reduce friction; sliding rough surfaces past each other has a warming effect (slip is dissipative, grip is not).
learnerActions: Rub your hands together quickly and feel them warm up — notice that sliding (slip) between surfaces produces heat.
Discuss grip: push gently on a shoe (or block) resting on a path and notice it does NOT slide until you push hard — static (grip) friction is balancing your push before the object moves.

Sort example situations into grip (prevents sliding: walking without slipping, standing on a slope without sliding, a parked object on a slope held in place, brakes holding) and slip (slows an existing slide: a sledge stopping, a skidding object).
Discuss friction as both helpful (grip lets us walk and lets brakes work) and unhelpful (slows a sledge) so friction is not labelled simply 'bad'.
activities.intendedInsight: Friction has two faces. Grip (static friction) can act on a still object WHEN something pushes it or it rests on a slope — it balances that push up to the point the object starts to slide. Slip (sliding friction) slows an object already sliding and warms the surfaces. Friction is both helpful and unhelpful depending on the situation.

activities.title: Shiny is not the same as slippery (predict–observe–explain)
feedback: If a learner predicts the shiny foil will be slippery and is surprised, name the lesson: shiny but rough still grips — shininess was a distraction.
Keep the variable clean: compare smoothness vs roughness, and do not compare a rolling object with a sliding one as if they were the same.
If asked about tray vs glass, steer toward the surfaces in contact (how rough/smooth they are and what they are made of), not how they look; testing is the way to find out.
activities.rationale: A predict–observe–explain contrast that deliberately crosses shininess with roughness separates the two, directly confronting the 'shiny = slippery' confusion and reinforcing roughness as the real cause.
sourceClaims: Rough surfaces have more friction than smooth surfaces; lubricants reduce friction; sliding rough surfaces past each other has a warming effect (slip is dissipative, grip is not).
learnerActions: Take two surfaces: crumpled-then-flattened kitchen foil (shiny but rough) and a sheet of matte-smooth card (dull but smooth).
Predict which lets the same block slide further, and say WHY before testing.
Slide the block on each with the same push and observe which surface lets it slide further; in most setups the block grips the crinkled shiny foil more and slides further on the smooth dull card.
Explain what your results suggest mattered (usually roughness, not shininess) and restate that friction is a force from the surfaces opposing motion.
Extra challenge: would a coin slide the same on a shiny metal tray and a shiny sheet of glass? Discuss what really decides it.
activities.intendedInsight: Shininess does not determine friction; what matters is the surfaces in contact: mainly how rough or smooth they are, and also what they are made of. 'Shiny = slippery' is a trap.

activities.title: Consolidate and check: sort, order, and explain
feedback: Full response: 'The block stops sooner on the rough carpet; the rough surface produces more friction — a force between block and surface acting against its motion; the smooth table has less friction so it slides further.'

If a learner says the block stopped because 'the push ran out' with no mention of the surface, re-run the same push on two surfaces so the only difference is the surface, forcing them to attribute the different distance to friction (reteach pushes-as-forces if the link is missing).
If a learner only says 'rough = slow, smooth = fast' as a surface property, push for the force language: the surfaces rubbing push back against the motion.

If a learner claims a pushed-but-still block has no friction, introduce grip (static): with nothing pushing there is no horizontal friction, but a shoe or block will not slide until pushed hard — static friction is balancing the push before movement.

Watch for backwards reasoning: 'it took a long time to stop, so friction was small' only holds if the test was fair (same object, same push, only the surface changed); otherwise ask what else could have changed, such as the push or the object.
activities.rationale: Ordering, categorising and explaining consolidate the pattern and are readily assessable, while the two-tier diagnostic discriminates the everyday view (push ran out / sticky / shiny) from the force view. These check and classify understanding but do not themselves generate the core insight or elicit the hands-on comparison.
sourceClaims: Many students see friction as a phenomenon rather than as a force; when two surfaces are in contact there is a force on each surface acting to stop them moving past one another.

The friction misconception has two mirror forms (friction only when moving / only when still); IOP teaches grip (prevents sliding, e.g. lets us walk) and slip (slows sliding and warms surfaces); friction can't be shown as a concrete entity so use force arrows; avoid reasoning backwards from effect to cause.
learnerActions: Order a set of surfaces by how far the object slides on each (furthest → stops soonest).
Sort everyday situations into friction that is helpful (walking, braking) versus unhelpful (slowing a sledge).
Match each surface to a grip or slip description.

Answer the diagnostic: 'I slide the same wooden block across a smooth table and across a rough carpet, giving the same push each time. On which surface does it stop sooner — and what about that surface stops it?' Give the mechanism, not just the outcome.
Reason about a still object: if you push gently on a block resting on a table but it does not move, is any friction acting on it? How could you tell (what happens as you push harder)?
activities.intendedInsight: A full understanding names friction as a FORCE between the two surfaces, acting opposite the motion and larger on rough surfaces, predicts the stopping order for a new pair of surfaces, and recognises that friction can also act on a still object being pushed or on a slope (grip/static friction balancing the push).

constraints: Keep the test fair: use the SAME object and the SAME push, change only the surface, and measure distance travelled.
Do not compare a rolling object with a sliding one as if equivalent — rolling resistance and sliding friction differ; keep the comparison to sliding.
Separate shininess from roughness deliberately (e.g. shiny-rough foil vs dull-smooth card); do not let learners treat 'shiny' as 'low friction'.

Address both mirror misconceptions: friction can act on a still object that is being pushed or on a slope (grip/static) as well as on a sliding one (slip); do not present it as only-when-moving or only-when-still. Also do not imply a free-standing object with nothing pushing it on a level surface has horizontal friction — it does not.
Present friction as both helpful and unhelpful, not simply 'bad'.

Sorting/ordering/matching and multiple-choice tasks consolidate and assess understanding but do not, on their own, produce the comparison that generates the insight; use them after hands-on or simulated trials.

An annotated static scene (shoe on ice vs path, brake on wheel, lift-the-flap friction facts) is a useful reference aid, but it cannot run the same-object-across-surfaces comparison; treat it as a recap, not the main investigation.
A screen simulation can show warming (a glowing meter) but cannot let learners feel heat; pair any simulation with real hands-rubbing/warming play.

A 2D runway fully captures the comparison and the arrow representation at this age; a 3D ramp would add realism but only use it if a 3D tilt/aim element is itself a learning goal, not as a substitute for the friction comparison.

Only infer friction from stopping distance inside a fair test (same object, same push, only the surface changed). Outside a fair test, avoid backwards reasoning from effect to cause (e.g. 'stopped slowly, so friction was small'), because a bigger push or a different object could explain the slow stop instead.
Role-play/open dialogue adds little for this specific objective: friction here is learned by comparing motion and visualising the opposing force rather than by talking in role.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three IOP sources carry verified:false in the source row (the grip/slip/drag sequence and the 'visualising grip and slip' page); treat their claims as cited but not independently re-checked here.

Force-direction care: friction opposes the direction of sliding and causes slowing; it is not the direction of travel and does not determine it. In these activities the object is given a push and then slows, so the opposing-arrow description is sound; if extending to objects that change direction, state the initial velocity explicitly.

Static-friction (grip) care: a still object with no applied push on a level surface has NO horizontal friction. Static friction only acts to balance an applied push or a slope's pull, up to the point the object starts to slide. The original assessment probe ('is there any friction on a still block right now?') was ambiguous on this and has been reframed to include a gentle push; the grip sort examples were also adjusted so each one (walking, standing on a slope, parked on a slope, braking) involves an actual push or slope. Do not teach that friction is always present on any still object.
The 'push runs out' idea is an impetus misconception to confront, not to teach; it appears only as an error pattern and in feedback, never as a correct explanation.

Source NGSS note: friction is excluded from the K-PS2-2 assessment boundary and is treated qualitatively at elementary, connecting to 3-PS2-1 and formalised at MS-PS2 — retained as standards context, not as a learner instruction.
The legacy row asserts 3D 'adds nothing' and that conversation has 'no value'; these have been softened to scoped trade-offs for this objective and age rather than universal laws.

assess.poeTask: Offer two surfaces: kitchen foil crumpled then flattened (shiny but rough) and a sheet of matte-smooth card. Ask the child to predict which lets the block slide further and WHY. Many predict the shiny foil (shininess = slippery); seeing the block grip the rough foil separates roughness from shininess as the real cause.
probeDeeper: Is friction pushing on the block? If so, which way?
The block is sitting still on the table. Is there any friction on it right now? How could you tell?
A shiny metal tray and a shiny sheet of glass — will a coin slide the same on both? What actually matters?
assess.correctAnswer: It stops sooner on the rough carpet. The rough surface produces more friction — a force between the block and the surface that acts against the block's motion and slows it; the smooth table has less friction so the block slides further.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The block stops because the push you gave it ran out, not because of the carpet.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast the SAME push on two surfaces so the only difference is the surface — force the child to attribute the different distance to the surface. Reteach pushes as forces if the link is missing.
errorPatterns.distractor: The block stops because the push you gave it runs out — the surface doesn't matter.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Explains stopping with no reference to the surface; friction plays no causal role.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Friction is only there when something is moving — a still block has no friction.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce grip (static) vs slip (sliding): a shoe won't slide until you push hard — friction is there before it moves.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says a stationary block on a table or gentle slope has zero friction and can't explain why it doesn't slide.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Shiny surfaces are always more slippery — friction is about shininess.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Test shiny-rough vs dull-smooth so shininess and roughness are separated; keep only roughness as the variable.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts a shiny-but-rough surface (crumpled foil, glossy sandpaper) will be slippery.

responseLevels.gap: Attributes the difference to the push running out or to the surface being 'sticky/bumpy' with no force language, or claims shininess is what matters.
responseLevels.full: Explains friction as a force between the two surfaces that acts opposite to the block's motion and is greater on rough surfaces, predicts the stopping order for a new pair of surfaces, and recognises friction can also act on a still object (grip).
responseLevels.partial: Says the rough surface has more friction and stops the block sooner, but treats friction as a property of the surface or as only-when-moving — states 'rough = slow, smooth = fast' without describing friction as a force acting against the motion from the surfaces rubbing.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I slide the same wooden block across a smooth table and across a rough carpet, giving it the same push each time. On which surface does it stop sooner — and what is it about that surface that stops it?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Tier 1 (rough stops it sooner) most 7-year-olds get from experience. Tier 2 divides: a child who understands friction names it as a FORCE opposing the motion, caused by the two surfaces rubbing; a child with the everyday view says the block 'ran out of push', calls the carpet 'sticky/bumpy' as a property rather than a force, or blames shininess. Same observation, different mechanism.
